opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Unless a Grain of Wheat Falls to the Ground

Jesus said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains just a grain of wheat; but if it dies, it produces much fruit.”

This is a difficult Gospel for me, especially in this season of my life.

I have always understood “dying to yourself” as putting others before yourself—serving, helping, giving what you can, and being present when someone needs you. Service is not always physical. Sometimes it is simply sitting with someone who is afraid, listening to someone who is hurting, or helping another person feel less alone.

I work in healthcare part-time, and I try to live that out there. Illness can leave people feeling completely powerless. If I can enter a room and ease even a small part of someone’s fear or anxiety, I feel that I have done something meaningful.

For a long time, that understanding of service felt clear and steady to me. But lately this Gospel has become harder to sit with, because I am also moving through a deeply lonely period of my life.

I have been married for many years, and my husband is my primary companionship. We genuinely enjoy one another. Yet recently, while I was away working, he had the opportunity to spend the weekend with me and instead chose to ride with friends. It hurt more than I expected, and it revealed something deeper: I wanted to be chosen.

And once I noticed that, I realized it was not an isolated feeling. There have been other moments with family and friendships where I have felt that, when a choice was made, it wasn’t me. In quieter moments, I even find myself wondering how many people would come to my funeral, and whether I have failed to build the lasting relationships I long for.

Sitting with that honestly has been uncomfortable. It is one thing to speak about service and self-gift in the abstract; it is another to feel unseen in the very places where you hoped for closeness.

And yet, it is precisely in that tension—between giving myself to others and longing to be chosen—that this Gospel begins to speak differently.

Jesus is not saying that dying to ourselves means we cease to matter. He is not asking us to become invisible, to accept loneliness without complaint, or to give our lives away while pretending we have no needs of our own.

The grain of wheat is first a sign of Christ himself. He gives his life, and from that gift comes new life. When he calls us to follow him, he is inviting us to surrender whatever in us prevents us from loving in that same way.

And so I begin to wonder if my experience of loneliness is not separate from this Gospel at all, but actually a doorway into it.

Maybe what has to die is not me.

Maybe what has to die is the belief that my worth depends on whether I am chosen.

Maybe it is resentment. Maybe it is fear of rejection. Maybe it is the expectation that one person can meet all my need for companionship. Maybe it is the quiet belief that being useful is what earns me a place in other people’s lives.

These are much harder things to let go of.

I also have to remember that the fruit of a life is not measured by who stands at our funeral.

There are people we touch whom we will never see again—a frightened patient who felt calmer because someone stayed long enough to listen, a person who needed kindness on a difficult day, someone who felt less alone simply because they were noticed. They may never remember our names, but the fruit is still real.

At the same time, faith is not meant to sanctify loneliness. God created us for relationship. Wanting companionship, wanting friendship, wanting to be chosen by the person you love—these are not selfish desires.

So perhaps the Gospel is not asking me to deny that longing, but to let it be transformed.

Perhaps the grain falling to the ground is not about erasing ourselves, but about allowing an old way of living to end so something new can grow.

For me, this season may not simply be about enduring loneliness. It may be an invitation to risk a larger life—to seek connection, to reach toward others even when I fear they will not reach back, and to stop measuring my worth by how often I am chosen.

That is frightening, because seeds disappear into darkness before anything new is visible.

Maybe that is why Jesus used a seed.

We surrender something without yet knowing what will come from it.

So I hear this Gospel differently now. I do not hear Jesus saying, “You do not matter. Give more of yourself away.”

I hear him asking:

What in you needs to die so that something new can finally grow?

And perhaps that is a question for anyone who has ever felt lonely, forgotten, overlooked, or unchosen.

The seed does not die because it is worthless.

It dies because there is more life within it than anyone can yet see.
